hypothesis: If the claim holds, then in a phylogeny that includes cave-obligate species from both America and Europe, each cave species' nearest relatives are surface or cave species from its own continent, and cave species from the two continents do not group together as continent-spanning cave clades.
pass_criterion: On a dated or undated phylogeny with cave-obligate species from both continents, at least 90% of cave species have their sister lineage or nearest relative on the same continent, and no clade made up only of cave species contains both American and European members. A permutation test of continent labels must give p < 0.05 for same-continent affinity.
fail_criterion: Fewer than 60% of cave species have a same-continent nearest relative, or at least one well-supported clade (posterior probability of 0.95 or more, or bootstrap support of 90 or more) made up only of cave species contains both American and European species, or the permutation test gives p of 0.05 or more.
interpretation: Darwin's 'cave-animals of America' and 'of Europe' are read as troglobitic or cave-obligate species. 'Affinities' is read as phylogenetic nearest relatives (sister lineages), and 'continent' as the species' sampling region. No single public dataset with a file list and a DOI that I could fetch holds cave-obligate species from both continents with their phylogenetic placement. The only candidate I fetched, the Dryad dataset 'Data from: Phylogenomics and biogeography of North American Trechine cave beetles (Coleoptera: Carabidae)', is American only. It has no European species and no sampled surface relatives. Its outgroups are Trechus obtusus, T. humboldti and Trechoblemus westcotti, and the page does not give their origins. Naming it would test only half of the claim, a weakened version, so I have not named it. The Biodiversity Data Journal spider data paper covers Europe only. GBIF has no cave-obligate flag, so it cannot isolate troglobites.
no_dataset_reason: I found no public dataset that I could fetch and that holds cave-obligate species from both America and Europe together with their phylogenetic placement or nearest relatives. The nearest candidate was the Dryad dataset 'Data from: Phylogenomics and biogeography of North American Trechine cave beetles (Coleoptera: Carabidae)' (DOI 10.5061/dryad.sj3tx967w). I fetched it and found it American only, with no European taxa and no sampled surface relatives, so it cannot test the America-versus-Europe comparison. The European spider data paper (https://bdj.pensoft.net/article/38492/) covers Europe only. Naming either would test a weakened version of the claim.
